text.p: A half million merrymakers, exuberant and remarkably well-behaved, ushered in 1997 on Wednesday with the traditional ball drop in New York City's Times Square.
The drop of the brightly lit rhinestone-decorated ball, an 89-year-old tradition, was accompanied by 3,000 pounds of confetti and 20,000 pompoms and balloons, and was broadcast worldwide.

Times Square Business Improvement District officials, who put on the New Year's celebration, said the crowd in the 42nd Street and Broadway area numbered 500,000 or more. At least 2,600 police were on hand to provide security, a police spokesman said.

Over the past two years, Mayor Rudy Giuliani and Times Square area officials have shut down pornography shops and brought a new sheen to the Great White Way, renovating old theatres and bringing in family-style entertainment such as Disney's "Beauty and the Beast."

At least two revellers, an amorous couple in the fourth-floor window of an office building overlooking 42nd Street, were nearly overcome with the excitement of the occasion. They had started to disrobe when spotlights were turned on them, to the delight of the crowd below.
Mark Fois, of East Chester, New York, said he joined the crowd because "I have a list of things I have to do in my life -- now I can check one off."
His brother Bob chimed in, "This is the year they're going to turn Times Square around. This is the year to be in Times Square."
Police reported no serious crime or pickpocketing incidents among the crowd, but many revellers were shivering as temperatures hovered in the teens (minus nine to minus seven Celsius).
Officer Mike Donnelly, working the New Year's event for the third year, said "This is the most organised I've seen it."

Jennifer Vann, a gymnastics coach from Raleigh, North Carolina, said safety had been a consideration but she decided to come to the outdoor party. "It was much safer than I expected," she said approvingly.

Times Square Business Improvement District officials for the first time picked an honoured guest for the event, 88-year-old Oseola McCarty. She is a Mississippi laundress who gained world reknown for donating her life savings of almost $250,000 to a local university.
McCarty, visiting New York City for the first time, told reporters she had never before celebrated New Year's Eve because she normally goes to bed at dark.
